hints: Look closely at the left side of the diagram and the three long chains on the right. Notice the 3-carbon backbone joined to each chain by a C-O link.
Remember what bond joins glycerol to fatty acids, and think carefully about whether water is used up or made during hydrolysis.
walkthrough:
**Identify the big molecule**

Look at the shape. On the left there is a short 3-carbon backbone, that is glycerol. Attached to it are three very long hydrocarbon chains with lots of C-H bonds.

Each attachment is a -C-O- link, which is an ester bond. This is the classic structure of a triglyceride, a lipid.

**Recall what hydrolysis does**

This triglyceride was made by condensation, where 3 fatty acids + glycerol joined and released water:
$$triglyceride + 3H_2O \rightarrow glycerol + 3 \text{ fatty acids (in reverse)}$$ 
Hydrolysis is the exact reverse. It uses water to break the 3 ester bonds.

**List the products, not the reactants**

Because water is split to break the bonds, it is used up as a reactant. It does not appear as a product.

So we are left with only the building blocks: 1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids. That matches option C.

options.A: No nitrogen or amino groups are present in the diagram, so no amino acids are involved. This is a lipid, not a protein.
options.B: Wrong building blocks and wrong role for water. There are no amino acids here, and water is used up in hydrolysis, not produced.
options.C: Correct. Hydrolysis of the three ester bonds in this triglyceride releases three fatty acids and one glycerol.
options.D: The building blocks are right, but water is a reactant used to break the ester bonds, not a product of hydrolysis.
